name: Victoria Peak
label: Victoria Peak
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Victoria Peak'.
notes: The classic skyline view over the harbour from the Lugard Road lookout.

text.description: Victoria Peak is the tallest hill on Hong Kong Island, at 552 metres. Locals simply call it The Peak. The name also covers the surrounding area of parks, viewing places and homes. It photographs well because the height gives a wide outlook over Central, Victoria Harbour, Lamma Island and the other islands, so one frame can hold towers, water and hills. People have come here for the view and the cooler air since the 19th century. A governor's summer house went up around 1868, and the Peak Tram funicular opened in 1888, which made the slope much easier to reach. The summit itself carries a radio facility and is closed to the public, so the best pictures are taken from the public areas around it rather than from the very top. Start with a wide shot of the skyline and harbour, then move in for details such as a cluster of towers or a single island. Keep the horizon level, because the straight line of the water shows any tilt. Wipe your lens first, and if the view is hazy, wait a little.
text.geographic_location: Victoria Peak is on the western half of Hong Kong Island, rising above Central and Victoria Harbour.
text.directions_text: Travel up to The Peak area from Central; the Peak Tram has served the Peak since 1888. The summit is closed to the public, so use the phone icon on the map for your photos rather than trying to reach the top. The phone icon on the map is about 420 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole sweep of harbour and skyline, and the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. A telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out the towers of Central or a distant island.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 420 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Photograph the Peak's slopes and the nearby buildings by turning to face that direction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, depending on whether the sky or the city is more interesting. Include some foreground, such as trees or a railing, to give depth. For the wide view, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and detail. If haze softens the distance, try the telephoto, which often gives more contrast on far buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good time to try, as the light softens and the city lights come on. Use night mode once it is properly dark, and hold the phone against a solid surface to keep it still.

text.access_note: The summit is closed to the public.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon to dusk usually gives softer light and the city lights come on after dark.
Night mode and resting the phone on a solid surface help in low light.

name: Temple Street Night Market
label: Temple Street Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tin Hau Temple' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '天后廟 Tin Hau Temple' (way/103291792): middle (45 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Temple Street, Hong Kong'.
notes: Lively night market with stalls and street food.

text.description: Temple Street Night Market is one of the busiest night markets in Hong Kong, in the Yau Ma Tei and Jordan part of Kowloon. It is popular with visitors and locals alike and is usually crowded around dusk. The street was built in the Qing dynasty and takes its name from the Tin Hau temple on the site. The temple area is a quieter, more atmospheric option for a phone photo than the busy main stretch. From the front of the temple, where the market is split by the temple complex, you can frame the ornate roof and the hanging incense coils, with market and fortune-teller stalls beside them. The mix of old religious detail and bright stall lights is what makes the scene work. The market has more than a hundred stalls with colourful lights, so there is plenty of colour at dusk and after dark. If you want a wider view, two other spots may be worth a look. One is the red archway on Temple Street, which frames the lit stalls and neon signs. The other is the upper level of the Yau Ma Tei Multi-Story Car Park, which has been described as looking down over the stall canopies. However, one guide says the car park was demolished and the view is no longer possible, and it may also be closed or full of parked cars, so verify on site before relying on it. Keep to the edge of the walkway when you stop to shoot, as the street gets busy.
text.geographic_location: Temple Street runs through Yau Ma Tei and Jordan in Kowloon, Hong Kong. The night market sits around the Tin Hau temple that gave the street its name.
text.directions_text: Take the MTR to Yau Ma Tei station and leave by Exit C. The street is about one minute on foot from there. Jordan station Exit A also works, at about ten minutes on foot. Once you are on Temple Street, walk along the market to the Tin Hau temple, where the stalls are split by the temple complex. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the temple roof and the stalls beside it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the red archway or a view down from a height. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the hanging incense coils without stepping into people's way.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the temple, where the market is split by the temple complex). The temple's ornate roof and the hanging incense coils, with the market and fortune-teller stalls beside it. Walk to the Tin Hau Temple on Temple Street, where the market is split by the temple complex, to take the temple shots. From the front of the temple you can see the ornate roof and the hanging incense coils, with the market and fortune-teller stalls beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the temple roof on the upper line, with the incense coils and stall lights below. For a wider alternative, shoot the red archway on Temple Street so it frames the lit stalls and neon signs. A high view from the Yau Ma Tei Multi-Story Car Park is another option only if it is open, as one guide says it was demolished.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the neon and stall lights do not wash out. If your phone offers night mode, use it for the temple detail. Hold the phone steady against your body or a railing, as night mode needs a still moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk is when the market is lively and the lights come on, so arrive then and keep shooting as it gets darker.

text.access_note: The street is open to the public, but the temple is a place of worship, so be respectful. The car park viewpoint may be closed or no longer exist, so check on site.
claims_not_in_sources: Night mode works best with the phone held steady against your body or a railing.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop bright neon and stall lights washing out.
The Tin Hau temple is a place of worship, so visitors should be respectful.
Stopping to shoot at the edge of the walkway avoids blocking passers-by on a busy street.

name: The Peninsula Hong Kong
label: The Peninsula
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Salisbury Road Garden' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '梳士巴利道花園 Salisbury Road Garden' (way/236062122): middle (54 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/709674355: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Peninsula Hong Kong' (117 m across).
notes: Grand colonial-era hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui.

text.description:
The Peninsula Hong Kong is a landmark colonial-style luxury hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon. It opened on 11 December 1928 at the corner of Nathan Road and Salisbury Road, and its Italianate frontage still looks formal and elegant. In 1994 a 30-storey tower was added in a similar style, and the original front facade and forecourt were kept. The hotel is also known for its fleet of Rolls-Royces painted in the hotel's own green.

The busy street corner is the obvious place to photograph it, but it is crowded and full of traffic. From there you can look back at the hotel through the trees. The branches act as a natural frame and give the picture some depth that a flat street-level shot lacks.

Take a few frames at different zoom levels, and turn the phone upright to include more of the tower. If you visit before Christmas, the hotel's festive decorations are traditionally put up weeks ahead, so the street-level views look quite different then. Keep to the pavements and crossings whenever you step out to compare angles.
text.geographic_location: The hotel is in Tsim Sha Tsui, in Kowloon, Hong Kong, at the junction of Nathan Road and Salisbury Road.
text.directions_text: Start in Tsim Sha Tsui and head for Salisbury Road. Tsim Sha Tsui can be reached on foot or by local transport; walk the last part along Salisbury Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the hotel and the trees around it. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the facade closer and keep the branches as a frame. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer to the frontage, and hold the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Salisbury Road Garden (garden on Salisbury Road, looking back at the hotel). The hotel seen through the trees of the garden, a less crowded framing than the street-level view. The hotel is to the south-west of you, and from here you see it through the trees of the garden, a less crowded view than the one from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Let branches or leaves frame the top or one side of the picture, with the hotel's facade in the gap. Turn on the gridlines to keep the building straight. For a different view, take a second shot from Nathan Road at Salisbury Road, where you get the frontage and tower with the street in the foreground, or from Salisbury Road, where the facade fills the frame. At street level, use the pavement crossings and do not step into barriered areas or stand near traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and bright facade keep their detail, as the trees can make the scene look dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight suits the tree-framed view. For the festive decorations on the street-level views, go in the weeks before Christmas, but check what is up on the day.

text.access_note: The garden and surrounding pavements are public places, but the hotel itself is private, so check the official site before you go if you want to enter it.
claims_not_in_sources: Salisbury Road Garden is a public garden that can be entered on foot.
Daylight is the best time for the tree-framed view because the branches are easier to see.
Exposure may need lowering because the trees cast shade while the facade is bright.

name: Two International Finance Centre
label: Two IFC
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '尖沙咀海濱花園 Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade' (way/605420842): middle (392 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3826645: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'International Finance Centre' (483 m across).
notes: Tall harbourfront skyscraper that dominates the Central skyline.

text.description:
Two International Finance Centre, often shortened to Two IFC, is the taller of the twin towers on the Central waterfront. At 412 metres it is the second-tallest building in Hong Kong. It was completed on 18 October 2003 and stands beside its shorter sibling, One IFC (210 m), with a shopping mall and the Four Seasons hotel around the base. It is quoted as having 88 storeys, a lucky number in Cantonese culture, though floors such as the 14th and 24th are left out. The towers also turn up in films such as The Dark Knight.

It photographs best from across the water. From the Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade on the Kowloon side, the towers sit to the right of the frame, with the Central skyline and the Observation Wheel close by. The harbour in front gives you open space and a clean horizon line, so the tall shapes stand out and are easy to frame. Take a few wide shots of the whole skyline, then zoom in on the tower for a tighter picture.

If you want a different view, Tamar Park on the Hong Kong Island side gives a ground-level look at the towers beside the Central waterfront. The Rumsey Street Flyover offers a close, upward shot of both towers above the traffic. Check that the flyover is still open to pedestrians before you plan around it.
text.geographic_location: Two IFC stands on the Victoria Harbour waterfront in Central, on the north shore of Hong Kong Island.
text.directions_text: Once you are on the waterfront, face south-west across the harbour and the towers of Central will be in front of you. Two IFC itself is on the other side of the water, in Central on Hong Kong Island. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole skyline and the harbour. Then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Two IFC closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the tower look very small and distant, so keep it for the promenade itself or the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade (Kowloon waterfront, looking across the harbour to Hong Kong Island). The Two IFC towers sit to the right of the frame across Victoria Harbour, with the Central skyline and the Observation Wheel nearby. Two IFC is across Victoria Harbour to the south-west, in the right-hand part of the frame, with the Central skyline and the Observation Wheel nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line, so the tall tower gets most of the frame. Keep the harbour water at the bottom to give the picture depth. If the full skyline looks crowded, zoom in on the two towers. You can also try panorama mode to sweep along the whole Central waterfront. Tamar Park on the Island side is a good alternative for a ground-level view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the building lights don't wash out. Hold the phone steady against a railing, or against your body, for zoomed shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good choice. Once the lights come on, switch to night mode and keep still for the few seconds it needs.

text.access_note: The promenade is an open public waterfront space, but check the official site before you go for any closures or works; the office towers themselves are private, so enjoy them from outside.
claims_not_in_sources: Towers and skyline are lit up after dark, so dusk and evening photos show the buildings' lights.
The promenade can be busy in the evening, so you may need to wait for a clear spot at the railing.
Haze over the harbour can make the distant towers look softer on some days.

name: Avenue of Stars
label: Avenue of Stars
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '星光大道' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '星光大道 Avenue of Stars' (relation/14947605): middle (495 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14947605: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Avenue of Stars' (496 m across).
notes: Harbourfront walk with the Bruce Lee statue and film star handprints.

text.description:
The Avenue of Stars is a waterfront promenade in Tsim Sha Tsui, modelled on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and dedicated to people from Hong Kong's film industry. It first opened on 28 April 2004 and reopened on 31 January 2019 after three years of renovation. The walk is about 440 metres long. Plaques set into the ground honour the stars, and nine red pillars tell a hundred years of Hong Kong cinema. Along the way you will find a 2.5-metre bronze Bruce Lee, added in 2005, and a bronze Anita Mui, added in 2014. The Bruce Lee statue may stand in a different place from where older photos show it.

It photographs well because the railing looks straight across Victoria Harbour to the Hong Kong Island skyline. IFC and Bank of China Tower are among the towers you can pick out. Guides often call this the classic postcard view of the island from the promenade. Stand at the railing and use it as a leading line, with the skyline behind. For a second picture, turn round and frame the Bruce Lee statue with a little of the city behind him. The promenade can be busy around the evening light show, so arrive early for a clear spot at the railing. Opening hours and the show schedule can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Tsim Sha Tsui, on the Kowloon side of Victoria Harbour, along the waterfront by the New World Centre. It sits at the eastern end of a row of waterfront attractions that includes the Museum of Art, the Space Museum, the Cultural Centre and the Clock Tower.
text.directions_text: There are no stops listed for this spot, so head for the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront in Kowloon and ask for the Avenue of Stars. Walk along the harbour edge and look for the promenade beside the New World Centre. You can also enter from Salisbury Garden, where a large replica film-award statuette greets visitors. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full skyline and the railing, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, compressed shot of the Central towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (central railings between the Bruce Lee statue and the west seating areas, facing the Hong Kong Island skyline). The Hong Kong Island skyline across the harbour, with IFC and Bank of China Tower among the towers, usually framed by the promenade railing. From there the skyline fills the view across the harbour, with IFC and Bank of China Tower among the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the horizon on a lower line, so the skyline sits above the railing. Let the railing run into the picture as a leading line. If you want the Bruce Lee statue in the frame too, step back a little and include it at the side. As a second option, the terrace at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre shows the harbour and light show with the statue and skyline together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the lit towers do not burn out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and blue hour, before the Symphony of Lights show at about 8 pm.

text.access_note: This is an open public promenade, but opening hours and the light show schedule can change, and the show is cancelled in severe weather, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The promenade can be busy around the time of the evening light show.
Resting your elbows on the railing helps keep the phone steady in night mode.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep detail in a bright sky and lit towers.

name: Man Mo Temple
label: Man Mo Temple
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/319658451: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Man Mo Temple' (62 m across).
notes: Incense coils hang from the ceiling of this 19th-century temple.

text.description:
Man Mo Temple is the largest of the Man Mo temples in Hong Kong, and it sits on Hollywood Road in Sheung Wan. It was built in 1847 and is dedicated to two figures: Man Cheong, the god of literature, and Kwan Tai, the martial god. The two gods were traditionally favoured by scholars and students seeking success in the imperial exams. The main temple is one of three neighbouring blocks. Next to it are Lit Shing Temple, for all heavenly gods, and Kung So, an old assembly hall where community disputes were settled. The temple has been looked after by the Tung Wah Group of Hospitals since 1908, and it is a Grade I historic building and a declared monument.

It photographs well because of the contrast between the old temple and the busy city around it. Outside you get the façade and the street. Inside, if the interior is dim, a slower approach will help. Start with a wide shot from the street outside to show the temple in its setting. Then move to the phone icon on the map and step closer for details: carved and painted decoration, lanterns, and incense smoke if there is any drifting in the light. Move gently, as people come here to worship, and keep your phone low-key. Inside, if the light is low, hold still for a second before pressing the shutter. Some temples ask visitors not to photograph certain areas, so follow any signs.
text.geographic_location: Man Mo Temple is at 124–126 Hollywood Road in Sheung Wan on Hong Kong Island. It stands beside Lit Shing Temple and Kung So, which form one complex with it.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport stop at this spot, so head to Sheung Wan on Hong Kong Island and make your way to Hollywood Road, looking for numbers 124–126. The phone icon on the map is at the centre of the temple outline, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the façade and the street around it, then switch to the default lens (1x) for most shots. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as decoration and lanterns that you cannot get close to.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the building as a whole, shoot from the street or the courtyard around it, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the temple's vertical lines straight so the building doesn't lean. Try one wide shot with some of the street included, one medium shot of the entrance, and one close detail. Inside, frame lanterns or any incense smoke against the darker background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so highlights don't burn out against darker interiors. In low light, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or your body. If there is moving smoke, try a Live Photo to catch it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when it is not crowded, often earlier in the day, so you can take your time. Daylight suits the outside; if it is dim inside, use night mode as needed.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship and a declared monument, so dress modestly, keep quiet, and check the official site before you go for access and photography rules.

sources.title: Man Mo temples in Hong Kong

name: Star Ferry
label: Star Ferry
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '1915 Clock Tower' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '鐘樓 Clock Tower' (node/12830242539): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM N3999281458 (Star Ferry): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Iconic green-and-white ferries crossing Victoria Harbour.

text.description:
The Star Ferry is the green-and-white passenger ferry that crosses Victoria Harbour, and its Tsim Sha Tsui pier is one of the easiest places in Hong Kong to take a photo with real character. A boat sliding up to the pier, with the Hong Kong Island skyline behind it, makes a ready-made postcard. The old clock tower next to the pier adds a second subject, and it is useful as a backdrop when you want a picture of yourselves or your group with the pier.

The best-known angle is from the steps beside the 1915 Clock Tower. Standing there you look down on boats as they dock, so the ferry sits in the foreground and the skyline fills the background. If you want a different view, two other places work well. The Ocean Terminal Deck gives a higher angle looking down on the ferry as it comes in, with the harbour behind. The Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade shows the ferry crossing the open water, with the island skyline across the harbour.

For a phone, this is a patient, simple spot. Choose your angle, wait for a ferry to approach, and take several frames as it comes in, because the boat's position against the skyline changes quickly. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines, and keep the clock tower or the pier edge in the frame to give a sense of place. Check the ferry timetable and the sunset time on the day, as they can vary.
text.geographic_location: The Star Ferry pier is at Tsim Sha Tsui, on the Kowloon side of Victoria Harbour, facing the Hong Kong Island skyline across the water. The 1915 Clock Tower stands right beside the pier.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. For a close-up view, head to the Star Ferry pier on the Tsim Sha Tsui harbour edge. The steps are beside the 1915 Clock Tower, next to the pier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the ferry, the pier and the skyline together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single boat against the skyline. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the clock tower and the pier in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 1915 Clock Tower (steps beside the clock tower, next to the Star Ferry pier). The green-and-white ferry pulling into the Tsim Sha Tsui pier, with the Hong Kong Island skyline behind it. The steps beside the 1915 Clock Tower, next to the pier, are the close-up viewpoint and are separate from the phone-icon point. From those steps you look down at the green-and-white ferry pulling into the Tsim Sha Tsui pier, with the Hong Kong Island skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the incoming ferry in the lower half of the frame and let the skyline fill the upper half. Use the gridlines to keep the horizon level. For a different angle, the Ocean Terminal Deck gives a higher view down onto the ferry as it arrives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the ferry to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the buildings keep their detail. Take a burst of shots or a Live Photo as the boat docks, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the sunset time and the ferry operating hours before you go, as they vary. Pick a time when a boat is arriving.

text.access_note: The steps are not listed as a paid viewpoint, but check the official site for pier access and ferry times.

pin_flags: not in OSM by Wikidata ID: pin kept

name: Bank of China Tower
label: Bank of China Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Statue Square' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '皇后像廣場 Statue Square' (relation/6970394): middle (177 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25604760: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bank of China Tower' (93 m across).

text.description:
The Bank of China Tower is one of Hong Kong's most recognisable landmarks, in the middle of Central on Hong Kong Island. It was designed by I. M. Pei and finished in 1990. It is 315 m tall, or 367.4 m with its two masts, and was the tallest building in Asia from 1990 to 1992. Its shape is made of triangular frameworks under glass walls, so the outline changes as you move around it. Some people see a meat cleaver in it, and it has the Cantonese nickname 'one knife'.

The tower photographs well because the glass and sharp angles give you strong lines and reflections against the Central skyline. The best ground-level view of the whole building is from Statue Square, an open plaza where nothing blocks the view. It is a short walk from the tower. Stand there and you can fit the full height in the frame with plenty of sky around it.

If you want something different, try a low, close shot from Garden Road beneath the footbridge. For a night view across the water, Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade shows the lit tower among the other Central skyscrapers.

A small observation deck on the 43rd floor used to be open to visitors, but it is not a reliable option now. Check before you plan around it.
text.geographic_location: In Central, on Hong Kong Island, at 1 Garden Road. The tower stands between Cotton Tree Drive and Garden Road, close to Chater Garden.
text.directions_text: From Central station on the MTR, take Exit J2 and walk through Chater Garden towards the tower. For the Garden Road angle, walk on to the footbridge area near Cheung Kong Center. Confirm the exact spot on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole tower with the skyline around it. If the top is cut off, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out the glass and triangular pattern near the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Statue Square. The full height of the tower against the Central skyline, from an open plaza with nothing blocking the view. From this open plaza you see the full height of the tower against the Central skyline, with the tower to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Line the tower up on a vertical grid line and leave a little sky above the masts. Keep the phone level so the edges do not lean. For a more dramatic shot, go to Garden Road under the footbridge. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) there to catch the angular facade with the footbridge framing it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the glass keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: On a clear day the glass picks up the sky, which gives clean, bright pictures. After dark, the lit facade looks striking, especially from Garden Road or across the harbour.

text.access_note: Statue Square and the street views are open to everyone, but the tower is a working bank headquarters, so check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside or up to the 43rd-floor deck.
claims_not_in_sources: Statue Square is an open public plaza that visitors can normally walk into freely.
On a clear day the glass facade reflects the sky.
Night mode works better when the phone is held steady against the body.
The full height may not fit in the default lens (1x) view from Statue Square, so the ultra-wide (0.5x) may be needed.

name: Central–Mid-Levels escalator
label: Mid-Levels Escalator
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Staunton Street' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '士丹頓街 Staunton Street' (way/1000056336): point nearest the subject (123 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21912378: large area 'Central-Mid-Levels Escalator System' (699 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The world's longest covered outdoor escalator system.

text.description:
The Central–Mid-Levels escalator is a chain of covered escalators and moving walkways that carries people up the steep slope of Hong Kong Island from Central towards the Mid-Levels. It is about 800 m long and climbs more than 135 m, which makes it the second longest outdoor covered escalator system in the world. It opened on 15 October 1993 and is made up of 18 escalators and three moving walkways. It helped turn the streets alongside it into the SoHo restaurant and bar district.

It photographs well because it is a working part of the city rather than a staged view. Everyday life passes right beside it: people riding, walkers overtaking on the moving walkways, and shopfronts and bars on both sides. The most natural shot is at street level on Staunton Street, where a pedestrian walks alongside the escalator with the SoHo bars and shopfronts behind. For a different view, Shelley Street offers a raised angle on the covered escalator climbing the stepped street, with the buildings around it in one frame.

The roof is partly translucent, so the light under it is soft. Keep the escalator as a leading line, add one person for scale, and wait a moment for a clear gap. The escalator runs downhill in the early morning and uphill from 10 a.m., so the direction of travel depends on when you visit.
text.geographic_location: On Hong Kong Island, running between Central and the Mid-Levels, from Queen's Road Central up towards Conduit Road. The Staunton Street stretch sits in the SoHo area, beside the escalator.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot, so start from Central and walk or take a taxi up to Staunton Street in SoHo. Follow the covered escalator itself and you will not lose your way. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a walker beside the escalator with the SoHo shopfronts around them. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in narrow spots such as Shelley Street to fit the whole stepped street and roof in. A 2x zoom, if your phone has one, helps you pick out one person without stepping into the flow.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Staunton Street (Staunton Street in the SoHo area, beside the escalator where it passes at street level). A pedestrian walking alongside the escalator at street level, with the SoHo bars and shopfronts visible beside it. From here you can photograph a pedestrian walking alongside the escalator, with the SoHo bars and shopfronts visible next to them. The main escalator lies to the north-east of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the escalator along one third of the frame, with the walker on a crossing point of the lines. Keep the shopfronts and bar signs in the background to show you are in SoHo. For an alternative, Shelley Street gives a raised view of the covered escalator climbing the stepped street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the walker to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright street behind makes the shot too light. If people move through quickly, take a few shots in a row, or try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards. After dark, night mode helps, but hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After 10 a.m. the escalator runs uphill; in the early morning it runs downhill. The SoHo bars are likely to be livelier in the evening.

text.access_note: The escalator and Staunton Street are open to the public, but check the official site before you go for current operating hours, direction of travel and any closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The SoHo bars are likely to be livelier in the evening.
Holding the phone against a wall or railing helps steady a night-mode shot.

name: Peak Tram
label: Peak Tram
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kennedy Road' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '堅尼地道 Kennedy Road' (node/526904599): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3264047: large area 'Peak Tram' (1275 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic funicular railway climbing to Victoria Peak.

text.description: The Peak Tram is a funicular railway that has carried people from Central up to Victoria Peak since 1888, and it was the first funicular in Asia. The line runs about 1.4 kilometres and climbs just under 400 metres, so the green tram spends much of its journey slanting across the hillside above the streets. That slope is what makes it work as a photo subject. This stand-here point is a quieter alternative, since a guide describes it as lesser-known with very few tourists. It is on Kennedy Road, one of the four intermediate request stops. Here the tram runs overhead at a diagonal while red taxis pass underneath, so you get movement above and traffic below in one frame. Kennedy Road is named after Arthur Edward Kennedy, a former Governor of Hong Kong, and after 1956 a spare tram car was kept in a car shed near the Kennedy Road station. The tram reopened on 27 August 2022 after a long renovation. Use the default lens (1x) for the tram and the street together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the structure above you in the picture. Wait for a taxi to pass before you press the shutter. If you have time, two other points on the line are worth a look: the stone bridge overlook on MacDonnell Road, and Barker Road beside the old arched station.
text.geographic_location: On Hong Kong Island, on the slopes of the Mid-Levels between Central and Victoria Peak. The spot is at the Kennedy Road stop of the Peak Tram.
text.directions_text: Start from Central or Admiralty, where the tram's lower terminus is on Garden Road near St John's Cathedral. From there, you can ride the tram and get off at the Kennedy Road request stop, since it is one of the tram's four request stops, or walk up from Garden Road, heading uphill (generally south-west) on the Mid-Levels slope. Check the official site before you go to see how the stops are running. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the tram and the street below it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the overhead structure. The telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) is useful for a tighter shot of the tram car.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kennedy Road (at Kennedy Road Peak Tram station, where the tram runs overhead). The green tram suspended diagonally above Kennedy Road, with red taxis passing below it. From there you look up at the green tram suspended diagonally above the road, with red taxis passing below it. The tram line itself continues up the slope to the south-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the diagonal of the tram along one of the lines, with the road filling the lower part of the frame. Wait for a taxi to pass beneath the tram so that both are in the shot. If you want a different view, the MacDonnell Road stone bridge overlook shows the tram climbing the slope with greenery and old tracks in front. Barker Road shows it coming out of dense trees beside the white arched station.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tram to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky behind it looks washed out. Live Photos can catch the tram and taxis moving, and you can choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose daylight, when you can see the tram's green colour and the taxis clearly. On cloudy days, shooting midway up the line is often better than going to the summit, which can be in cloud.

text.access_note: The tram and its stops are run by the operator, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Daylight shows the green tram and the red taxis clearly.
Taxis pass along Kennedy Road often enough that you can wait for one to pass under the tram.

name: Hong Kong Park
label: Hong Kong Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Edward Youde Aviary' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '尤德觀鳥園 Edward Youde Aviary' (way/114282518): middle (122 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/42255430: large area 'Hong Kong Park' (613 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Green park with waterfalls, a large aviary and skyscraper backdrops.

text.description: Hong Kong Park is a green pocket right in the middle of Central's towers, which is much of its appeal for photos: trees, water and pavilions with glass buildings rising behind. It opened on 23 May 1991 and covers about 8 hectares. The site was once part of the Victoria Barracks, and a few of the old buildings are still there. Flagstaff House, dating from 1846, is now a teaware museum. The park's best-known feature is the Edward Youde Aviary, the largest aviary in Hong Kong, and guides recommend it as a strong spot for bird photography. From the walk-through aviary you can get close to tropical birds, with the netted structure, the park's pavilions and the trees behind them. Two other views are worth a look. The Artificial Lake has its waterfall in the foreground, with the Admiralty and Central towers over the greenery. The Vantage Point gives a wider view across the gardens and lake, framed by tower blocks. Work out where the light falls before you start, and keep your phone lens clean, as the humid air can leave a film on it. Take a few frames of each scene, with and without people, and check them before moving on. Some areas may have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Hong Kong Park is in Central, on Hong Kong Island, beside Cotton Tree Drive. It sits between the business towers of Admiralty and Central, close to Pacific Place.
text.directions_text: The park sits beside Cotton Tree Drive. You can walk in through Pacific Place and its nearby escalator. Once inside, follow the paths towards the pond and pavilions to find the Edward Youde Aviary. The middle of the park is about 150 m to the north-east of the aviary, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for birds, and the default lens (1x) for the wider aviary and pavilion scenes. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) at the lake to fit the waterfall and towers into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Edward Youde Aviary (inside the park, near the pond and pavilions). Tropical birds and the aviary's netted structure, with the park's pavilions and trees in the background. From here you can photograph tropical birds with the aviary's netted structure, and the park's pavilions and trees behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Be patient: wait for a bird to settle, then frame it with greenery behind. For a wider shot, include the pavilions and trees. If you have time, the Artificial Lake gives a good second view, with the waterfall in front and the Admiralty and Central towers behind. Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level against the tall buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bird to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky behind is bright. Try Live Photos to catch the moment a bird moves. Portrait mode can blur the background if you are close to a bird, but it does not always cope well with netting, so check the result.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a dry day when the park is quieter, and check the light on the lake and towers before you set up.

text.access_note: Hong Kong Park is a public park and the aviary is described as free to enter, but check the official site before you go for current access rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The humid air can leave a film on a phone lens, so it is worth wiping it before shooting.
A phone's autofocus can lock onto the aviary netting rather than the bird, so tapping on the bird helps.
The park is usually quieter on a dry day, and light on the lake and towers changes through the day.
Portrait mode may struggle with netting in front of a subject.

name: Tai Kwun
label: Tai Kwun
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parade Ground' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '檢閱廣場 Parade Ground' (way/544485290): middle (99 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/591035975: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tai Kwun' (225 m across).
notes: Restored colonial police station and prison turned arts centre.

text.description:
Tai Kwun is the former Central Police Station compound, a cluster of Victorian and early twentieth-century buildings in the middle of Central. The three declared monuments here are the old police station, the Former Central Magistracy and Victoria Prison. The 16 historic buildings were put up between 1841 and 1925. Victoria Prison was decommissioned in 2006. The compound reopened to the public on 29 May 2018 as a centre for heritage and arts. Two new buildings were added, with designs inspired by the old brickwork.

It photographs well because old and new sit close together. The classic picture is taken on the Parade Ground, where the red-brick Barrack Block fills the frame behind the open ground. If you have time, two other corners are worth a look. In the Prison Yard, the dark modern JC Cube block stands against the century-old granite prison walls. At the Laundry Steps, visitors sit on the stepped structure, with plain grey concrete walls and strong lines behind them.

All three spots are at ground level inside the site, so you will not get a view down over the compound. Indoor light is dim, so keep most of your photos for the courtyards. Opening hours can vary, so check the official site on the day.
text.geographic_location: Tai Kwun is in Central, on Hong Kong Island. It is surrounded by Hollywood Road, Arbuthnot Road, Chancery Lane and Old Bailey Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Central and then for Hollywood Road, which is one of the roads around the compound. Check the official site or a map app for the best way in. Once inside, walk onto the Parade Ground, the open ground in front of the red-brick Barrack Block. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Barrack Block as a Victorian backdrop. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as brickwork and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parade Ground (middle of the open ground, facing the red-brick Barrack Block). The red-brick Barrack Block filling the frame as a Victorian backdrop, with the open lawn-like ground in the foreground. In the middle of the open ground, facing the red-brick Barrack Block. That puts the brick building across the frame with the open, lawn-like ground in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the long brick facade level along one of the horizontal lines, leaving the open ground in the lower third. Hold the phone upright for height or sideways for width. For a second picture, go to the Prison Yard and frame the dark modern JC Cube against the old granite walls. The Laundry Steps are another option, with people sitting on the stepped structure and the grey concrete lines behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Indoors, where the light is dim, hold the phone steady and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed time is needed. Softer daylight in the morning or late afternoon usually suits the red brick best, and the Parade Ground is easier to photograph when it is less busy.

text.access_note: Tai Kwun is a heritage and arts site with open courtyards, but opening hours can vary and some exhibitions need tickets, so check the official site on the day.

name: International Commerce Centre
label: ICC Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenue of Stars' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '星光大道 Avenue of Stars' (relation/14947605): middle (495 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25590249: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'International Commerce Centre' (114 m across).
notes: Hong Kong's tallest building, in West Kowloon.

text.description:
The International Commerce Centre, or ICC, is Hong Kong's tallest building: 108 storeys and 484 m high, finished in 2010. It stands in West Kowloon on top of the Elements mall, and its south side faces Victoria Harbour. The tower was designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox with Wong & Ouyang. Its height was scaled back from an earlier plan, because buildings were not allowed to rise above the surrounding mountains.

One recommended view is from the Avenue of Stars, in the Arena of Stars section. Here the tower rises beside the promenade's statues and the harbour, and the Hong Kong Island skyline sits across the water. A guide describes this stretch as a golden-hour spot where the statues and the tower fit into one frame. That gives your photo a foreground, a middle and a skyline, rather than just a tall building.

The tower is also used for a large LED light and music show on two of its facades. Check locally for show times before you plan around it. Keep the tower upright in the frame, use the gridlines to keep the edges straight, and leave some space above the roof so the top is not cut off. A second viewpoint, the Central Waterfront Promenade, shows the tower across the harbour with the Central business district and the Kowloon skyline.
text.geographic_location: The tower is in West Kowloon, Hong Kong, on top of the Elements mall and close to Kowloon and Austin MTR stations. The suggested viewpoint, the Avenue of Stars, is a waterfront promenade on the Victoria Harbour side of Kowloon, to the south-east of the tower.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop itself, so take a taxi and ask for the Avenue of Stars, or walk from the nearest convenient transport. If you would rather see the tower up close, it sits above Elements mall, next to Kowloon station (Airport Express and Tung Chung line) and Austin station (Tuen Ma line). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the statues, the harbour and the tower in one frame. If the tower looks small, try the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring it closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the statues large in the foreground, and keep them away from the edges so they don't stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenue of Stars (Arena of Stars section, looking back toward Central). The ICC rises beside the promenade's statues and the harbour, with the Hong Kong Island skyline across the water. The ICC is to the north-west of here. From the promenade, the tower rises beside the statues and the harbour, with the Hong Kong Island skyline across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a statue or the promenade rail in the foreground, and the tower behind it. Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Leave a little sky above the roof. For a different view, the Central Waterfront Promenade shows the tower across the harbour with the Central business district and the Kowloon skyline in the same shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Stay with the default lens (1x) or a gentle zoom, and hold the phone steady against the rail or with both elbows tucked in. After dark, use night mode and keep still for the full exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, the golden hour, according to the guide. Go a little early so you can try a few angles before the light changes.

text.access_note: The Avenue of Stars is a free, open waterfront walk, but check the official site before you go in case sections are closed or changed.

name: Hong Kong Observation Wheel
label: Observation Wheel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tamar Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '添馬公園 Tamar Park' (way/138602057): middle (291 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/323202866: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Hong Kong Observation Wheel' (64 m across).
notes: Giant Ferris wheel on the Central harbourfront.

text.description:
The Hong Kong Observation Wheel stands on the Central Harbourfront, right beside Victoria Harbour. It is about 60 metres tall and has 42 gondolas. A ride takes about 15 minutes, with two to three turns. It was built on reclaimed land between Central Pier No. 9 and Pier No. 10, and it opened in late 2014. After a dispute between operators it reopened on 20 December 2017 as part of the AIA Vitality Park.

The wheel photographs well because it is a clean, round shape against open water and sky. That keeps the picture simple and uncluttered.

The wheel is a large subject, so a phone does best when you pick one idea per spot. From the park, use the default lens (1x) for the whole wheel with some waterfront around it. Move in with the telephoto if you want a tighter shot. For a different view, try the footbridge towards Jardine House, where the wheel sits about level with you among the city and the traffic. Another option is Central Pier No. 9, where you can stand close and shoot upwards. Access to those two places may have changed since the guidance was written, so look at the signs on the day.
text.geographic_location: On the Central Harbourfront in Central, Hong Kong, on the edge of Victoria Harbour between Central Pier No. 9 and Pier No. 10, next to the AIA Vitality Park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so find your own way to the Central Harbourfront, where the wheel stands, for example by checking a map app. Walk the waterfront from the wheel towards HKCEC, covering about 600 m. Then turn round and look back towards Central Pier and the wheel. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from Tamar Park to show the whole wheel with open harbour around it. If your phone has telephoto (2x-3x), try it for a tighter, more graphic shot of the wheel alone. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you are close to the wheel, for example at Central Pier No. 9.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Tamar Park (reached by walking the waterfront from the wheel toward HKCEC, then looking back toward Central Pier). The wheel against the open harbourfront with no skyscraper behind it. From there the wheel is to the north-west. Walk the waterfront from the wheel towards HKCEC, then turn and look back towards Central Pier. The wheel stands against the open harbourfront with no skyscraper behind it, which makes this a quieter, cleaner view than the busy city backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the wheel on one of the vertical lines, leaving some water or sky on the other side. Keep the horizon level so the harbour does not slope. For a different view, try the footbridge towards Jardine House, where the wheel sits about level with you amid the city and traffic, or Central Pier No. 9, where you can shoot upwards from close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wheel to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the wheel does not turn into a silhouette. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against a railing or your body to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest time to be on the waterfront. If you want the wheel lit up and light trails from the footbridge, wait until after dark.

text.access_note: The waterfront around the wheel is mostly open public space, but riding the wheel is ticketed, and access to the footbridge and pier may change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter on the waterfront.
The wheel is lit after dark, so it shows up well in night photos.
Telephoto on a phone gives a tighter view of the wheel; the exact zoom range (2x-3x) depends on the phone.
Gridlines and tap-to-focus with the exposure slider are available in most phone camera apps.

name: Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade
label: TST Promenade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenue of Stars' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '星光大道 Avenue of Stars' (relation/14947605): middle (495 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM W605420842 (Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfront walk with the best view of the Hong Kong Island skyline.

text.description:
Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade is the railed harbourfront walkway on the Kowloon side of Victoria Harbour. It is one of the easiest places in Hong Kong to photograph the Central skyline across the water. From the middle section of the Avenue of Stars, facing Hong Kong Island, the railing and walkway sit in the foreground and the towers of Central rise behind them. Several guides call this the classic postcard view of the promenade. That foreground gives the picture depth, and a phone copes well with the wide scene because the subject is large and the open water leaves nothing to get in the way.

The spot is also popular for watching the nightly Symphony of Lights show, which guides say runs at 8 PM. The waterfront gets very crowded beforehand, so arrive early if you want a place at the rail. For a quieter visit, the Avenue of Stars is said to be much calmer at sunrise, though the skyline is less lit then. Which section is best is a matter of taste, so check on the day: some favour the stretch nearest the Star Ferry, while others say that is the busiest part.

If you want a different view, try the Tsim Sha Tsui Clock Tower. It puts the red-brick tower in the foreground, with the promenade, the harbour and the Hong Kong Island skyline beyond. Another option is the eastern end of the promenade, where buildings stacked closely along the waterfront give a compressed skyline.
text.geographic_location: In Tsim Sha Tsui, on the Kowloon waterfront of Victoria Harbour, looking across the water to the Central skyline on Hong Kong Island.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront area and head to the harbour edge. From there, the middle of the promenade is about 600 m to the west. Follow the harbourfront railing and keep the water on your side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the railing with the skyline behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowd stops you stepping back, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a group of towers across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (middle section of the walkway, facing Hong Kong Island). The promenade's railed harbourfront walkway in the foreground, with the Central skyline across Victoria Harbour behind it. Walk west along the harbourfront to the middle section of the Avenue of Stars and face Hong Kong Island. The photo shows the railed harbourfront walkway in the foreground, with the Central skyline across Victoria Harbour behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the railing along the lower third so it leads the eye along the walkway. Leave the skyline across the upper two thirds, and keep the horizon level. If the Clock Tower is your alternative, put the red-brick tower in the foreground and let the promenade and skyline sit beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit buildings do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise is said to be much quieter on the Avenue of Stars, though the skyline is less lit then. The Symphony of Lights show runs nightly at 8 PM and the waterfront gets very crowded before it, so arrive early to claim a spot.

text.access_note: This is a public harbourfront walkway, but check the official site before you go for any works, closures or event arrangements.

name: HSBC Main Building
label: HSBC Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Statue Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '皇后像廣場 Statue Square' (relation/6970394): middle (177 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27008054: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'HSBC Main Building' (119 m across).
notes: Norman Foster's high-tech landmark on Statue Square.

text.description: The HSBC Main Building is the Hong Kong headquarters of The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, designed by Norman Foster and finished in 1985. It is easy to spot in Central because the structure is on show. Steel masts and big triangular trusses sit on the outside, and the whole tower is hung from them rather than built around a solid core. It stands 178.8 metres high with 47 storeys. At the time it was the most expensive building in the world, and its steel modules were prefabricated in Britain and shipped to Hong Kong. That makes it a good subject for a phone. The lines are strong and repeat, the glass and metal catch the light, and the open plaza in front gives you room to step back. The classic picture is the full front of the tower rising above the square, with the bronze lions near the entrance in the foreground. Stand square-on and use the gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight. Include a little paving or a lion at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale. If you want a quieter angle on the tower, try Charter Garden. The building is best photographed from outside, as photography inside is restricted.
text.geographic_location: In Central, on the north shore of Hong Kong Island. The building stands on the southern side of Statue Square, at 1 Queen's Road Central.
text.directions_text: From that point, the tower is to the south-west, about 184 m away and roughly 3 minutes on foot. For the classic frontal view, face the entrance across Des Voeux Road Central from the lions. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the tower. If the top gets cut off, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the sides do not lean in. A telephoto lens (2x-5x) is good for close shots of the trusses and steel masts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Statue Square (Directly facing the building's front, across Des Voeux Road Central from the lions). The full front elevation of the tower rising over an open plaza, with the bronze lions in the foreground near the entrance. For the classic frontal view, the recommended viewpoint is Statue Square, facing the front of the building across Des Voeux Road Central from the lions. From there you see the full front of the tower rising above an open plaza, with the bronze lions in the foreground near the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's vertical edges up with them. Hold the phone upright rather than tilting it up, as tilting makes the sides lean inward. Keep a strip of plaza or one of the lions at the bottom of the frame for foreground. For a different angle, try Charter Garden, which shows the tower from the garden side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the steel frame stays clear. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady so the lit tower stays sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the tower is lit and the plaza is open in front of you. Daylight also works well for showing off the steel structure.

text.access_note: Only interior photography is noted as restricted, and the ground floor sometimes hosts exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hong Kong Cultural Centre
label: Cultural Centre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '尖沙咀海濱花園 Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade' (relation/12919867): edge nearest the subject (1210 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37664345: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hong Kong Cultural Centre' (176 m across).
notes: Distinctive sloped-roof building on the Kowloon waterfront.

text.description: The Hong Kong Cultural Centre is a large performing-arts venue on the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront. Its curved, sandy-coloured outer wall and leaning pillars make a strong shape against the harbour. From the promenade to the east, the centre can appear at a distance with the harbour and the Hong Kong Island skyline beside it. The centre was designed by José Lei and officially opened on 8 November 1989 by Charles, Prince of Wales and Princess Diana. It stands on the site of the old Kowloon railway station, and pulling that station down was very controversial at the time. Inside is a 2,019-seat Concert Hall with an 8,000-pipe organ, described as the largest in Asia. Most visitors only need the outside for photos. The Star Ferry pier and the historic Clock Tower are close by, so you can easily add a second shot of the Clock Tower with the centre and the harbour behind it. Let the centre sit on one side of the frame and the harbour and skyline fill the rest. Stand near the railing for a more open composition. The promenade gets very crowded before the nightly Symphony of Lights show, so arrive early if you want a clear spot. One guide recommends blue hour, about 15 to 30 minutes after sunset.
text.geographic_location: The centre is on Salisbury Road at the southwestern tip of Tsim Sha Tsui, on the Kowloon side of the harbour, facing Hong Kong Island. It sits next to the Star Ferry pier, the Clock Tower, the Hong Kong Space Museum and the Hong Kong Museum of Art.
text.directions_text: The centre itself is within walking distance of Tsim Sha Tsui station (Tsuen Wan line) and East Tsim Sha Tsui station (Tuen Ma line), and it is right beside the Star Ferry pier. If you would rather not walk, a taxi to the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront also works. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so you can fit the centre, the harbour and the skyline in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the centre itself or parts of the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade (waterfront stretch beside the Cultural Centre, facing Hong Kong Island). The Cultural Centre's exterior wall in the foreground with the Hong Kong Island skyline and harbour across the water. From here the centre appears at a distance, with the harbour and skyline beside it, rather than filling the foreground. Standing near the waterfront railing gives you a clearer, more spacious frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line, with the centre as a distinctive shape on one side and the harbour and skyline filling the rest. Keep the verticals straight by holding the phone level, since tilting makes the pillars lean even more. For a different view, try the Clock Tower with the Cultural Centre nearby and the harbour behind it, or use the telephoto to pick out the curved, sandy-coloured exterior with the harbour glimpsed beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the sky or the skyline to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly so the lights across the water don't blow out. After sunset, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone still. Tripods can be restricted here, so don't count on one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide suggests blue hour, about 15 to 30 minutes after sunset. Arrive early, because the waterfront gets very crowded before the nightly Symphony of Lights show.

text.access_note: The promenade is an open public waterfront, but photography is generally not allowed inside the halls during performances, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Tsim Sha Tsui is on the Kowloon side of Victoria Harbour.
Resting your elbows on a railing helps keep a phone steady in night mode.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall vertical lines look as if they lean.

name: Golden Bauhinia Square
label: Golden Bauhinia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Expo Promenade' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '博覽海濱花園 Expo Promenade' (way/744299949): middle (158 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/744299949: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Expo Promenade' (158 m across).
notes: Golden bauhinia statue on the Wan Chai waterfront.

text.description:
Golden Bauhinia Square is an open waterfront space in Wan Chai, outside the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. It is named after the gilded bauhinia flower statue at its centre, which stands about six metres high on a red granite base shaped like a pillar on a pyramid. The convention centre is where the 1997 handover ceremonies were held, so the statue has become an important symbol for many people in Hong Kong. Locals have also nicknamed it the "Golden Pak Choi".

It photographs well because the bright gold flower and deep red base stand out against the water, with Victoria Harbour opening up behind. From the centre of the square, in front of the statue, you get the classic shot that most visitors come for. A flag-raising ceremony is held here every day at around 8 a.m., which draws a crowd, so arrive early if you want a clear view of the statue. Early morning and near sunset are the times guides suggest for softer light and fewer people.

If you have time, walk along the Expo Promenade for a second view: Kowloon and the Tsim Sha Tsui skyline across the harbour, with the square nearby. The waterfront can be windy, so hold your phone with both hands. Some visitors report vendors near the statue offering paid photos; you can politely ignore them and take your own.
text.geographic_location: Golden Bauhinia Square is in Wan Chai on the north shore of Hong Kong Island, on the waterfront beside the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre.
text.directions_text: Start from Wan Chai and head north towards the harbour and the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. The square is on the waterfront outside the centre. If you are coming from further away, you could go by taxi and ask for the Golden Bauhinia Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the harbour behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole square and the sky, and use telephoto (2x-5x) for a tighter shot of the flower on its base.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Expo Promenade (waterfront edge beside the square, facing Victoria Harbour). Kowloon and the Tsim Sha Tsui skyline across the harbour, seen from the Hong Kong Island side, with the bauhinia square nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving the water and sky behind it. Crouch slightly and tilt the phone up a little to make the statue look taller, but keep the phone level to avoid leaning edges. For a second view, walk along the Expo Promenade and photograph the Tsim Sha Tsui skyline across the harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gold of the statue to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the gilding keeps its detail against the bright sky. Wipe the lens first, as the waterfront air can be damp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or near sunset, when the light is softer and it is usually quieter. The daily flag-raising ceremony is around 8 a.m. and draws crowds, so get there before it starts if you want the statue to yourself.

text.access_note: This is an open public waterfront square, but check the official site before you go for ceremony times and any temporary closures.

name: St John's Cathedral
label: St John's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Garden Road' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '花園道 Garden Road' (way/636324517): middle (177 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107497695: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. John's Cathedral' (68 m across).
notes: The oldest Anglican church in the Far East, set among towers.

text.description:
St John's Cathedral is the Anglican cathedral of Hong Kong Island. It sits in a pocket of grounds and trees on Garden Road, with Central's towers all around it. It was consecrated in 1852 and is the oldest surviving Western church building in Hong Kong. It was declared a monument in 1996. The style is a plain version of 13th-century English Gothic, so the exterior has a calm, simple look that stands out against the glass and steel nearby. The bell tower carries a large "VR" for Queen Victoria, and a memorial cross (a Celtic cross) stands beside the building. Both make good details to look for.

From the pavement you can take in the whole exterior across the road, with the grounds and trees in front. It is a quieter, more road-level view than the entrance courtyard. If you want the classic shot of the Gothic front framed by the Central skyscrapers behind, walk over to the courtyard outside the main entrance and shoot wide.

The cathedral is an active place of worship and weddings are held often. Avoid flash, and do not photograph during services. Check the cathedral's website for events before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Central, on Hong Kong Island, on Garden Road. It sits among the Bank of China Tower, the HSBC Main Building and the Court of Final Appeal Building, and directly across from the Peak Tram lower terminus.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Central and head for Garden Road and the Peak Tram lower terminus. From there the cathedral is to the north-east, about 200 m away (a few minutes on foot). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cathedral seen across the road. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if trees or traffic force you close, or if you move to the courtyard for the front view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bell tower and its details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Garden Road (opposite the cathedral, near the Peak Tram lower terminus). The cathedral's exterior seen across the road, with the grounds and trees in front of it. Opposite the cathedral near the Peak Tram lower terminus. The cathedral is to the north-east, and from here you see its exterior across the road with the grounds and trees in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the tower upright by lining it up with a vertical grid line. Use the trees and grounds as a foreground layer so the building does not float. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a second angle, the courtyard outside the main entrance shows the Gothic front with the Central towers behind, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens suits it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral's stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Do not use flash, especially near services.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Avoid service times and wedding slots; check the cathedral's website for events.

text.access_note: The cathedral is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and events, and avoid flash and photography during services.
